Core exam idea

The material repeatedly connects the rise of Vijayanagara with a changing political landscape: Delhi's weakening influence, local resistance, and opportunities created by the decline/defeat of existing southern powers.

Remember the triangle

  • V.E. = Vijayanagara Empire
  • B.K. = Bahmani Kingdom
  • D.S. = Delhi Sultanate

Poster 03

Origin story: why did Vijayanagara emerge?

Follow the cause → opportunity → consolidation chain instead of memorizing isolated facts.

1 • Political opening

The source frames the weakening of the Delhi Sultanate and the disruption of older southern powers as an opening for new regional kingdoms.

2 • Southern power base

The lecture connects Harihara I and Bukka I with the foundation phase and places Hoysala and the Sultanate of Madurai among the major surrounding powers.

3 • Strategic consolidation

Control of fertile and economically valuable zones, especially river/Delta regions, becomes a recurring theme in the conflict story.

Source image 10

Harihara I — foundation frame

Political opportunity + military challenge are highlighted as the two major starting pressures.

Vijayanagara rulers: the must-remember chain

First memorize the dynasty sequence, then attach rulers and events to it.

Sangama
→
Saluva
→
Tuluva

Aravidu

Harihara I

1336 — the material presents him as the key foundation/coronation figure.

Bukka I

1356–1377 — associated with expansion and the continuing contest with Bahmani and Madurai powers.

Harihara II

1377–1404 — the material emphasizes the eastern-coast turn and the Warangal/Bahmani relationship.

Deva Raya I

1406–1422 — linked with continued Tungabhadra struggle and a Bahmani challenge.

Deva Raya II

1425–1446 — source notes emphasize reforms, military context and renewed contest around the Krishna–Godavari zone.

Why did Vijayanagara and Bahmani keep fighting?

The source repeatedly reduces the rivalry to geography + fertility + economic value + strategic control.

Tungabhadra Doab

Presented as fertile and economically valuable, with the Western Chalukyas–Imperial Cholas and Yadavas–Hoysalas cited in the conflict background.

Krishna–Godavari delta

Highlighted as fertile and economically important — therefore a region of interest to competing powers.

Marathwada

The source links the region with fertility and ports, adding another economic/strategic reason for rivalry.

Poster 06

Bahmani Kingdom: origin → rulers → breakup

Use the source's own sequence to connect Bahmani formation with the wider Deccan story.

Foundation

The material gives 1347 AD and associates the foundation with Ala-ud-din Hasan Bahman Shah, also called Hasan Gangu in the source notes.

Expansion & conflict

The Bahmani state becomes a principal rival of Vijayanagara, especially around fertile frontier zones.

Later fragmentation

The material connects the Bahmani decline with the emergence of Deccan successor states.
